The Brown tang (Zebrasoma scopas) is a widely distributed surgeonfish inhabiting coral reefs across the Indo-Pacific region, where it plays an important role in controlling algal biomass. Field measurements of adult specimens indicate that individuals can attain a maximum total length of 40 centimeters [Li = 40 centimeters], a dimension that places this species among the medium-sized members of its genus. This asymptotic size is achieved through a prolonged growth phase that spans several years, with most somatic expansion occurring during the juvenile and early adult stages. The relationship between length and body mass in this species follows a typical power function for acanthurids, with mature individuals reaching an ultimate wet weight of 3329 grams [Wwi = 3329 grams] at the upper end of the size range. Such a substantial body mass is associated with a relatively high food intake requirement, as these fish graze almost continuously on filamentous algae and detritus throughout daylight hours. The largest recorded specimens are typically collected from shallow, high-productivity zones where food resources are abundant and competition from other herbivores is moderate.

Reproductive development in Zebrasoma scopas is characterized by a distinct size threshold that marks the transition to sexual maturity, with individuals reaching puberty at a total length of 13.2 centimeters [Lp = 13.2 centimeters]. At this length, the corresponding body mass is approximately 112 grams [Wwp = approximately 112 grams], a value derived from the species-specific length-weight regression. This pubertal size is achieved relatively early in the lifespan, allowing individuals to begin contributing to the next generation well before attaining their maximum dimensions. The onset of gonadal activity is accompanied by a suite of physiological changes including vitellogenesis onset and the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Field surveys of spawning aggregations in Micronesia have shown that fish below this size threshold are rarely observed participating in reproductive events, suggesting that body size acts as a reliable predictor of reproductive status in this species. Comparatively, the size at puberty in Z. scopas is smaller than that reported for the congeneric Zebrasoma veliferum, which matures at nearly 18 centimeters.

Reproductive output in the Brown tang is substantial when considered over the course of a single spawning season, with females releasing a large number of pelagic eggs during each broadcast spawning event. Under laboratory conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], females produce approximately 21100 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 21100 eggs per spawning event], with an average of about one spawning event per week [F_R_i = about one spawning event per week]. This yields a maximum daily reproductive rate of approximately 3014 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 3014 eggs per day] at 28 °C. This high frequency of gamete release is sustained over several months during the peak breeding season, which typically coincides with periods of elevated water temperature and increased primary productivity. The daily reproductive rate implied by this intense spawning activity is among the highest recorded for acanthurid fishes of comparable body size, reflecting an energy allocation strategy that prioritizes continuous, low-investment offspring production over the production of fewer, larger clutches. Such a strategy is well-suited to an environment where larval survival is highly unpredictable and where density-independent mortality factors dominate during the pelagic larval phase.

The earliest life stages of Zebrasoma scopas are characterized by extremely small size, reflecting the minimal maternal investment per offspring that is typical of broadcast-spawning teleosts. Newly hatched larvae emerge from transparent, pelagic eggs with a wet weight at birth of just 0.00023 grams [Wwb = 0.00023 grams], a minuscule starting mass that necessitates rapid yolk absorption and an early transition to exogenous feeding. This neonatal mass is derived from an egg diameter of approximately 0.75 millimeters, which is consistent with values reported for other chaetodontoid and acanthurid species that produce small, free-floating eggs. The yolk-sac larva, or prolarva, relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves for the first 48 to 72 hours post-hatching, during which time the mouth gape opens and the retina differentiates in preparation for first prey capture. Upon completion of yolk-sac resorption, the exotrophic transition occurs, and the larva begins feeding on small planktonic organisms such as copepod nauplii and rotifers. This period of early larval development is the most vulnerable phase of the life cycle, with mortality rates exceeding 95 percent in the first week alone.

Longevity records for Zebrasoma scopas suggest that individuals can survive for several decades under favorable reef conditions, with the maximum recorded lifespan estimated at 41 years [am = 41 years] when maintained at a water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This exceptional longevity is unusual among small-to-medium sized surgeonfishes and positions Z. scopas as a relatively long-lived species within the Acanthuridae family. The capacity for such extended survival is likely facilitated by the species' robust immune defenses, low natural predation rates upon reaching adult size, and the consistent availability of dietary algae across its tropical reef habitat. In comparison, the congeneric Zebrasoma flavescens has a reported maximum lifespan of only 30 years, suggesting that subtle differences in metabolic rate and reproductive scheduling may underpin these interspecific differences. The 41-year lifespan observed in the Brown tang implies that individuals may participate in reproductive activity for over three decades, given that puberty is reached well before the halfway point of the potential lifespan. This protracted reproductive window, combined with the species' high daily reproductive output, contributes to the remarkable population resilience observed in healthy, unfished reef systems.
